Smart
SMART
v.i. (to suffer pain, especially as consequence; of the man who goes surety for a stranger)
From Old English smeortan, to be painful. At Proverbs 11:15 it renders Hebrew ra'a, to be broken or brought to evil — the older English sense of smart as a stinging pain rather than cleverness.

Biblical Definition

Solomon returns to the subject of standing surety more often than to almost any other piece of financial counsel, and always the same way: He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure. The English holds a pun the Hebrew does not, and it is a useful one — to smart is to sting, and the man who guarantees a stranger's debt will feel it. Proverbs 6 opens with the same warning and treats it as an emergency: if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger, go, humble thyself, and make sure thy friend... deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter. Get out tonight; do not give sleep to thine eyes.

The word is worth the entry for the older sense of smart, which has almost vanished from English. It means to feel a sharp consequence, and Scripture uses consequence as an ordinary instrument of instruction without apology. Proverbs is largely a book of them: the sluggard and his poverty, the drunkard and his woes, the adulterer and his wounds and dishonour. None of this is fatalism, and none of it denies grace. It is the created order's ordinary way of teaching, and a father who removes every consequence from a son's path is not being kind to him. What Proverbs will not do is let the sting be the last word. The book that says the surety shall smart for it is the same book that says a friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): to feel a lively pungent pain; to feel the punishment or evil consequence of anything.

expand to see more

SMART, v.i. To feel a lively pungent pain; to feel a pungent pain of mind; to feel the punishment of error or wrong.

SMART, n. Quick pungent lively pain; a pricking local pain, as the pain from puncture by nettles.

SURETISHIP, n. The state of being surety; the obligation of a person to answer for another.

SURETY, n. Security against loss or damage; one that is bound with and for another.

STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not of the family.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 11:15 — "He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it: and he that hateth suretiship is sure."

Proverbs 6:1 — "My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger,"

Proverbs 22:26 — "Be not thou one of them that strike hands, or of them that are sureties for debts."

Hebrews 7:22 — "By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament."

Modern Corruption

Consequence is treated as cruelty, and a generation shielded from every sting arrives at adulthood without the instruction Proverbs assumes a father will let life give.

expand to see more

A wide instinct now holds that a loving parent, church or society removes the sting from error. Proverbs assumes the opposite as a matter of course: the surety smarts, the sluggard goes hungry, the scorner finds no one to teach him. This is not harshness but the way a wise God built the world to instruct creatures who do not learn well from advice. The Reformed doctrine of the law's first use says the same thing in another register — the law restrains and exposes before it ever guides, and a man who has never felt its edge will not look for a Saviour.

The remarkable thing is where the Bible takes the word. Proverbs spends three warnings telling a man never to become surety for a stranger, because he will smart for it; and Hebrews says that Jesus was made a surety of a better testament. He did the one thing Solomon said no wise man should do. He struck hands for strangers — for those who were strangers from the covenants of promise — and He smarted for it to the last farthing. Proverbs describes the cost so that the reader will know what it meant when Christ paid it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ra'a (H7489), to be broken, to suffer harm; arab (H6148), to go surety; taqa kaph (H8628 / H3709), to strike the hand.

expand to see more

Hebrew ra'a (H7489) — to be broken, to come to evil; the AV's shall smart for it.

Hebrew arab (H6148) — to pledge, to go surety; the same verb as Hezekiah's undertake for me.

Hebrew taqa kaph (H8628, H3709) — to strike the hand; the gesture that sealed a guarantee.

Hebrew zar (H2114) — a stranger, an outsider; the party Proverbs warns against guaranteeing.

Greek egguos (G1450) — a surety; the title given to the Lord Jesus in Hebrews 7:22.

Usage

"“He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it” — the sting named in advance."

"“deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter” — Proverbs treating it as an emergency."

"“Jesus made a surety of a better testament” — the one who did it anyway."
